accuracy.reason: All eight cards distinguish discovery from service health and trust; TTL and failure-cache limits avoid false cutover guarantees. Illustrative reserved hierarchy is explicitly non-public.

evidence.quote: Some resolvers can even serve expired data when refreshing fails, so TTL is not a hard global recovery deadline.

mechanisms.reason: Actors, referral sequence, alias/address dependency, positive/negative cache aging and separate health steering are traceable; diagrams preserve resolver ownership and no-push semantics.

evidence.quote: The negative answer has its own cache lifetime; the new positive record's TTL does not clear it.

coherence.reason: Names and records precede resolver hierarchy, aliases, cache changes, negative results, failover, diagnosis and trust. Conceptual boundaries accumulate usefully.

evidence.quote: Name discovery and serving the HTTP request are separate steps.

decisions.reason: Planned overlap, TTL query costs, replacement capacity, diagnosis order and certificate checks turn mechanisms into concrete operational choices.

evidence.quote: West must be reachable, healthy and have enough spare capacity for redirected work.

clarity.reason: Defines unfamiliar DNS vocabulary before use; examples isolate alias lookup and stale address lifetime, while clear boundaries prevent health and encryption confusion.

evidence.quote: DNSSEC protects DNS data; HTTPS protects the connection to the requested service identity.

outcomes.reason: Cards 1-3 support hostname versus path, stub/recursive/authority roles, delegation/referrals, cache shortcuts, A/AAAA families and CNAME target dependency/separate caching. Learner correctly traces the changed names and later HTTPS.
Card 4 supports old TTL surviving edit, 11:59+3600=12:59, advance lowering, overlap/traffic monitoring and shorter-TTL query costs; learner rejects a universal retirement deadline.

Card 5 supports negative lifetime independent of new positive TTL, NXDOMAIN versus NODATA type scope, and SERVFAIL as potentially cached resolution failure rather than absence. All criteria appear in learner.
Card 6 supports separate health/policy action, lookup/request split mismatch, persistent caches/connections, no instant migration and reachable healthy spare capacity. Learner covers each.

Card 7 teaches cached/open-connection survival, fresh resolution dependencies, recursive/name/type/error/TTL then authoritative/delegation checks, HTTP-500 separation and limits of redundancy. Learner preserves uncertainty about actual cause.
Card 8 supports signed-data origin/integrity chain, no DNS query encryption or health guarantee, and requested-hostname HTTPS identity/encryption. Learner keeps the checks separate after aliases.

sourceChecks.claim: Cloudflare DNS explanation supports hostname discovery before connection; address discovery does not carry the later HTTP path/exchange.
AWS lookup walkthrough and RFC 1034 support recursive referral following, authoritative zone data and cached shortcuts; teaching hierarchy is correctly labeled illustrative.
AWS record reference confirms A/IPv4, AAAA/IPv6 and name-valued CNAME; RFC 1034 alias resolution supports obtaining target addresses.
RFC 8767 confirms ordinary TTL aging with exceptional serve-stale beyond expiry. Old entries are not rewritten by authoritative edits; overlap and non-instant cutover follow.
RFC 9520 and referenced RFC 2308 distinguish NXDOMAIN/NODATA from resolution failure and require failure caching; negative lifetime is independent of a later positive record.
AWS failover uses separate health checks to select DNS answers; DNS cache/connection reuse limits traffic precision and speed, and cannot provide application capacity.
RFC 1034 describes resolver/authority/cache dependencies and redundant authoritative service; shared wrong data and later HTTP failures remain separate concerns.

RFC 4033 confirms origin/integrity authentication without confidentiality or application validation. RFC 9525 independently confirms service identity derives from the requested source hostname rather than an alias target.
